title: A playbook is not a pedagogy
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes reflects on a mistake she made leading PD at scale for the first time: producing an elegant instructional playbook that changed little in classroom quality, because playbooks without intellectual preparation are 'mostly paper architecture'. She argues trusts confuse uniformity ('did I see the strategy?') with coherence ('was the teaching decision sound, given the learning, the pupils and the subject?'), and that subject knowledge changes what a technique even means - modelling in English is not modelling in maths. Her core proposal is that every playbook should require teachers to consider five questions before choosing a technique: the learning problem, the likely difficulty, the evidence of understanding, the support needed, and the in-the-moment decision that might follow. She closes by arguing CPD sessions on modelling, checking for understanding or scaffolding should explore the thinking behind the technique, not simply demonstrate the technique itself.
points: Hughes's confession that her own trust-wide instructional playbook produced 'little change in classroom quality' lends unusual candour and authority to her critique of playbook-driven school improvement.

Her distinction between uniformity ('did I see the strategy?') and coherence ('was the teaching decision sound?') gives leaders a precise diagnostic for telling genuine improvement from performative compliance.
Her claim that 'subject knowledge changes the technique' - modelling in English differs from modelling in maths - challenges generic, subject-neutral instructional frameworks directly.

Her five-question framework (learning problem, likely difficulty, evidence of understanding, support needed, in-the-moment decision) offers a concrete tool leaders can embed directly into existing playbooks.
quotes: This is the big mistake I made this year when leading PD at scale for the first time. A multi-academy trust can create the most elegant instructional playbook in the sector and still see little change in classroom quality.
Uniformity asks, Did I see the strategy? Coherence asks, Was the teaching decision sound, given the learning, the pupils and the subject?
Modelling in English is not the same as modelling in maths. Reading in history is not the same as reading in science. Subject knowledge changes the technique.

Every playbook should ask teachers to consider five things before choosing the technique: What is the learning problem? What is the likely difficulty? What evidence will show understanding? What support will preserve ambition? What decision might I need to make in the moment?
The playbook is the visible object. The intellectual preparation is the work. Without it, lesson principles become another set of words staff learn to repeat. With it, they become a way of thinking.
